phy_edx.11.0.summary: Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**: **unlike poles attract** and **like poles repel**, and only a magnet repelling another object proves that object is a magnet. The **magnetic materials** are **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**; steel and cobalt alloys keep their magnetism, so they make **permanent magnets**, while soft iron is easily magnetised and demagnetised, so it is used for **temporary (induced) magnets** such as electromagnet cores. An **induced magnet** only becomes magnetic while it is in a magnetic field, and the force between an induced magnet and a permanent magnet is **always attraction**.

core.p: The **poles** of a magnet are the regions where its magnetic field is strongest and where the magnetic force is greatest. Every magnet has two poles: a **north (north-seeking) pole** and a **south (south-seeking) pole**.
bullets: Freely suspended, a bar magnet turns until its **north-seeking pole** points to the Earth's geographic north.
Poles always come in pairs: cut a bar magnet in half and you get **two smaller magnets**, each with its own N and S pole.
The field (and force) is strongest at the poles, which is why paper clips cluster at the ends of a bar magnet, not the middle.
Magnetic forces are **non-contact forces**: they act across a gap, even through paper, wood or plastic.

callouts.p: A region of a magnet where the magnetic field is strongest; every magnet has a north pole and a south pole.

core.p: The rule you must **recall** is short: **unlike poles attract** and **like poles repel**. N and S pull together; N and N, or S and S, push apart.
bullets: N near S: **attract**.
N near N: **repel**. S near S: **repel**.
The force gets **weaker as the distance between poles increases**.
The forces are a **pair**: each magnet pushes or pulls the other with an equal-sized force in the opposite direction.

callouts.p: Unlike poles attract; like poles repel.

core.h: Repulsion is the only proof of a magnet
core.p: A piece of unmagnetised iron is attracted to **either** pole of a magnet, so attraction cannot tell you whether something is a magnet. Only **repulsion** proves it, because only two magnets can repel.
bullets: Test: bring each end of the unknown bar up to the **N pole** of a known magnet, then to the **S pole**.
If one end is **repelled** by a pole, the bar is a magnet (like poles face each other).
If it is attracted by both poles at both ends, it is just a **magnetic material** (unmagnetised).
The repelled end has the **same** name as the pole that repelled it.

callouts.p: Write the word repel: 'attraction can happen with unmagnetised magnetic material, so only repulsion shows the object is a magnet'.

core.p: A **magnetic material** is one that is attracted to a magnet and can be magnetised. The Edexcel spec names four: **iron, steel, cobalt and nickel**. Steel is an alloy that is mostly iron.
bullets: **Iron** (especially soft iron): magnetises and demagnetises easily.
**Steel**: hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism.
**Cobalt**: keeps its magnetism well; used in strong permanent magnet alloys.
**Nickel**: magnetic; used in magnetic alloys.
Most metals are **not** magnetic: copper, aluminium, brass, gold, silver, lead and zinc are not attracted.
A steel can is attracted to a magnet; an aluminium drinks can is not, which is how recycling plants separate them.

callouts.p: Not all metals are magnetic. Aluminium and copper are metals but are not magnetic materials.

core.p: A **permanent magnet** produces its **own magnetic field** all the time, without needing anything else. It is made from a **magnetically hard** material such as **steel** or an alloy containing **cobalt** (or nickel), which keeps its magnetism once magnetised.
bullets: Always has a N and a S pole and its own field.
Can **attract or repel** another magnet.
Hard to magnetise, but also hard to demagnetise, so it stays magnetic for a long time.
Can be weakened by strong heating, hammering or dropping repeatedly.

callouts.p: A magnet that produces its own magnetic field.

core.p: An **induced magnet** is a magnetic material that **becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field**. When it is taken out of the field it **loses most or all of its magnetism quickly** (especially soft iron).
bullets: The magnetism is **induced** (caused) by the field of a nearby permanent magnet or electromagnet.
The end of the material nearest a N pole becomes an induced **S** pole, and vice versa.
Because the nearest induced pole is always the opposite type, the force between an induced magnet and the magnet causing it is **always attraction**.
A chain of paper clips hanging from a magnet works this way: each clip becomes an induced magnet and attracts the next.
Take the magnet away and the clips (iron/soft steel) fall apart.

callouts.p: A material that becomes a magnet when it is placed in a magnetic field.
The force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always attractive.

core.p: The key difference is whether the object makes its **own** field (permanent) or only becomes magnetic **while in another field** (induced).
bullets: Permanent: own field all the time; can attract **or** repel.
Induced: only magnetic while in a field; force on it is always **attraction**.
Induced magnet loses its magnetism when removed from the field; a permanent magnet does not.
Remove the cause: an induced magnet stops being a magnet; a permanent magnet carries on.

callouts.p: Permanent: produces its own field. Induced: becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field, loses magnetism when removed. Force between them always attraction.

core.p: Magnetic materials behave differently once the magnetising field is removed, and this decides what they are used for.
bullets: **Magnetically soft** (soft iron): easy to magnetise and **easy to lose magnetism**. Ideal where the magnetism must be switched on and off.
**Magnetically hard** (steel, cobalt alloys): harder to magnetise but **keeps its magnetism**. Ideal for permanent magnets.
Classic experiment: stroke or place a steel pin and an iron nail on a magnet, pick up clips, then remove the magnet. The steel keeps its clips; the iron drops them.
'Soft' and 'hard' describe magnetic behaviour, not how physically soft the metal is.

callouts.p: Do not say soft iron is used for permanent magnets. Soft iron loses its magnetism, so it is used for temporary magnets.

core.p: Use a permanent magnet whenever a **constant magnetic field** is needed without any electricity.
bullets: **Compass needles** (magnetised steel).
**Fridge magnets** and magnetic door catches.
**Loudspeakers and headphones** (permanent magnet interacts with a coil).
**Electric motors and generators** (fixed field magnets).
Magnetic stripes and some data storage, magnetic toys and sorting machines.
Strong permanent magnets often use alloys containing **cobalt** or **nickel** (e.g. alnico: aluminium, nickel, cobalt).

core.p: Use a temporary (induced) magnet, usually **soft iron**, when the magnetism must be **switched on and off** or must change quickly.
bullets: **Cores of electromagnets**: field is strong with current on and almost disappears when it is switched off.
**Scrapyard cranes**: lift steel cars, then drop them by switching off the current.
**Relays, electric bells and circuit breakers**: soft iron armature is attracted, then released.
**Transformer cores**: soft iron is magnetised and demagnetised many times each second.
Magnetic separation in recycling: iron and steel are picked out from aluminium and other waste.

callouts.p: Permanent use: steel or cobalt (keeps magnetism). Temporary use: soft iron (loses magnetism easily).

core.p: Six-mark and explain questions reward a **chain of reasoning**: name the material, say what happens to its magnetism, then link to the observation.
bullets: Use the words **induced**, **permanent**, **magnetic field**, **attract**, **repel**.
Say which pole is induced and why the force is attraction.
For choosing a material, state the property (keeps or loses magnetism) and link it to the use.
When describing a test, give both the method (bring near each pole) and the conclusion (repel means magnet).

callouts.p: Recall = state the rule. Describe = say what happens. Explain = say what happens AND why.

analogy.t: Magnets as a team and their fans
analogy.p: A permanent magnet is like a famous footballer who is always a star, wherever they go. An induced magnet is like a fan in the stadium who starts cheering (becomes magnetised) only while the star is near, always facing towards them (always attraction), and goes quiet once the star leaves. Soft iron is a fan who calms down instantly; steel is a fan who keeps chanting long after. Where it breaks down: real induced magnetism has a definite pole pattern (opposite pole nearest), and a magnet also exerts a force back on the material, which the fan picture does not show.

terms.d: Region of a magnet where the magnetic field and force are strongest; every magnet has a north and a south pole.
The pole of a freely suspended magnet that points towards the Earth's geographic north.
The pole of a freely suspended magnet that points towards the Earth's geographic south.
A force pulling two objects together; happens between unlike poles, and between a magnet and a magnetic material.
A force pushing two objects apart; happens only between like poles of two magnets.
A material attracted by a magnet that can be magnetised: iron, steel, cobalt and nickel.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time.
A material that becomes a magnet when placed in a magnetic field and loses most or all of its magnetism when removed.
Another name for a magnet whose magnetism disappears when the magnetising field is removed, e.g. soft iron.
Describes a material such as steel that is hard to magnetise but keeps its magnetism.
Describes a material such as soft iron that is easily magnetised and easily loses its magnetism.
The region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as the magnetic force.
Soft iron placed inside a coil to make its field much stronger; it loses magnetism when the current is switched off.

mistakes.w: All metals are magnetic.
mistakes.r: Only iron, steel, cobalt and nickel (and their alloys) are magnetic; copper and aluminium are not.

mistakes.w: The object was attracted, so it must be a magnet.
mistakes.r: Attraction also happens with unmagnetised magnetic material; only repulsion proves it is a magnet.

mistakes.w: Like poles attract.
mistakes.r: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet can be repelled by the magnet that induces it.
mistakes.r: The force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet is always attraction.

mistakes.w: Soft iron is used for permanent magnets because it is easy to magnetise.
mistakes.r: Soft iron loses its magnetism easily, so it is used for temporary magnets such as electromagnet cores; steel or cobalt is used for permanent magnets.

mistakes.w: An induced magnet keeps its magnetism after the magnet is removed.
mistakes.r: It loses most or all of its magnetism when removed from the field.

mistakes.w: A permanent magnet is one that is very strong.
mistakes.r: A permanent magnet is one that produces its own magnetic field; strength is not the definition.

mistakes.r: It becomes a south pole, so the nail is attracted.

exam.q: State what happens when the north pole of one magnet is brought near the north pole of another.
model: They repel (push apart).
exam.tip: Like poles repel.

exam.q: Name two magnetic elements.
model: Any two from: iron, cobalt, nickel (steel accepted as a magnetic material/alloy).
exam.tip: Learn the list of four: iron, steel, cobalt, nickel.

exam.q: Which of these is not a magnetic material? A iron  B nickel  C aluminium  D cobalt
model: C aluminium.
exam.tip: Watch for copper and aluminium as distractors.

exam.q: Explain the difference between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
model: A permanent magnet produces its own magnetic field (all the time).
An induced magnet only becomes a magnet when it is in a magnetic field / loses its magnetism when removed.
exam.tip: Use the words 'own magnetic field' and 'placed in a magnetic field'.

exam.q: A student says a metal bar must be a magnet because it is attracted to a bar magnet. Explain why the student may be wrong and describe a test that would show whether the bar is a magnet.
model: A magnetic material that is not magnetised is also attracted (to either pole).
Bring each end of the bar near the N pole and then the S pole of a known magnet.
If any end is repelled, the bar is a magnet.
If it is attracted in every case, it is an unmagnetised magnetic material.
exam.tip: Repulsion is the only proof.

exam.q: State the type of force between a permanent magnet and an induced magnet.
model: Attraction (always attractive).
exam.tip: Never repulsion.

exam.q: Explain why an iron nail is attracted to the north pole of a bar magnet.
model: The nail is placed in the magnetic field of the magnet so it becomes an induced magnet.
The end nearest the north pole becomes a south pole.
Unlike poles attract, so the nail is attracted.
exam.tip: Give the induced pole and the rule.

exam.q: Electromagnets in scrapyard cranes have cores made of iron, not steel. Explain why.
model: Iron is magnetically soft / loses its magnetism easily when the current is switched off.
So the crane can release (drop) the scrap metal; steel would stay magnetised and keep holding it.
exam.tip: Link property to purpose.

exam.q: A chain of paper clips hangs from a magnet. When the magnet is removed the clips fall apart. Explain these observations.
model: Each clip is in the magnetic field so becomes an induced magnet.
Each induced magnet attracts the next clip.
When the magnet is removed the clips lose their (induced) magnetism, so they no longer attract each other.
exam.tip: Induced magnets need the field to stay magnetic.

exam.q: Describe how permanent and temporary magnetic materials are used. Refer to iron, steel, cobalt and nickel in your answer.
model: Steel and alloys of cobalt/nickel keep their magnetism, so are used for permanent magnets.
Examples: compass needles, fridge magnets, loudspeakers, motors.
These are used where a constant field is needed without electricity.
Soft iron is easily magnetised and loses its magnetism easily, so is used for temporary magnets.
Examples: electromagnet cores, cranes, relays, bells, transformer cores.
Used where the magnetism must be switched on and off or reverse quickly.
exam.tip: Structure: material, property, use, reason. Do both permanent and temporary.

worked.q: Three bars X, Y and Z look identical. X repels one end of a known magnet. Y is attracted to both ends of the magnet. Z is not affected. Identify each bar.
steps: X is repelled, and only two magnets can repel, so X is a permanent magnet.
Y is attracted to both poles, so it is a magnetic material that is not magnetised (e.g. iron), becoming an induced magnet near the magnet.
Z is not attracted at all, so it is a non-magnetic material such as aluminium or copper.
worked.ans: X = magnet, Y = unmagnetised magnetic material (e.g. iron), Z = non-magnetic (e.g. aluminium).

worked.q: A designer needs a material for (a) the needle of a compass and (b) the core of a relay that must release its armature when the current stops. Choose and justify.
steps: (a) A compass needle must stay magnetised permanently to line up with the Earth's field: choose steel (magnetically hard).
(b) The relay core must lose its magnetism as soon as the current stops: choose soft iron (magnetically soft), which is an induced magnet only while the coil's field is present.
worked.ans: (a) Steel, because it keeps its magnetism; (b) soft iron, because it loses its magnetism easily.

phy_edx.11.1.summary: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet where a magnetic material or another magnet feels a force; we show it with **field lines** that point from **north to south**, never cross, and are **closest together where the field is strongest** (at the poles). Between opposite poles facing each other, the lines are parallel and equally spaced, giving a **uniform field**. **Plotting compasses** reveal the shape and direction of a field because their needles line up along the field lines, and the fact that a compass points north everywhere on Earth is evidence that the **Earth has a magnetic field like a bar magnet**, so its **core must be magnetic**.

core.p: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet in which a **magnetic material** or another **magnet** experiences a **non-contact force**.
bullets: The field is three-dimensional: it surrounds the magnet in every direction, not just in the plane drawn on paper.
The field is **strongest at the poles** and gets weaker with increasing distance from the magnet.
We cannot see the field, so we represent it with **magnetic field lines**.
The force acts on iron, steel, cobalt and nickel, and on other magnets.

callouts.p: The region around a magnet where a force acts on another magnet or on a magnetic material.

core.p: Field lines are a model: they show both the **shape** and the **direction** of the field, and their spacing shows its **strength**.
bullets: Lines go **from the north pole to the south pole** (outside the magnet).
Every line needs an **arrow** showing direction.
Lines **never cross** (the field can only point one way at any point).
Lines **start and end on poles**; they touch the magnet at the ends.
The **closer together** the lines, the **stronger** the field.
The direction of a field line is the direction a **north pole** (e.g. a compass needle's N end) would be pushed.

callouts.p: Field lines point from N to S. Field direction = direction of the force on a north pole.

core.p: Around a single bar magnet the lines **leave the north pole**, curve round, and **enter the south pole**. They are **most concentrated at the poles**, which is why the field and force are strongest there.
bullets: Shape: closed loops from N to S, curving round the sides of the magnet.
Lines **bunch together near the poles** (strong field) and **spread out** further away (weaker field).
Along the axis, lines come straight out of the N end and straight into the S end.
The pattern is symmetrical above and below the magnet.

callouts.p: Lines drawn without arrows, crossing each other or not touching the poles lose marks.

core.p: Edexcel wants you to **relate the strength of the field to the concentration of lines**: the more lines through a given area, the stronger the field.
bullets: Concentrated (close) lines = **strong field**: near the poles.
Widely spaced lines = **weak field**: far from the magnet.
Equally spaced lines = **same strength everywhere** (uniform field).
Iron filings sprinkled on paper above a magnet cluster most densely at the poles, showing this concentration.

head: Line pattern
Meaning
rows: Uniform field: same strength and direction

core.p: A **uniform field** has the **same strength and the same direction at every point**. It is made between a **north pole and a south pole facing each other** across a small gap (for example the flat poles of a U-shaped magnet).
bullets: Drawn as **straight, parallel, equally spaced lines** from N to S.
Arrows point from the N pole to the S pole.
Near the edges of the gap the lines bulge outwards (the field is not uniform there), but questions usually ask about the central region.
Uniform fields are used in the motor effect and F = BIl questions, so this pattern links forward.

callouts.p: A magnetic field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced field lines.

core.p: When two bar magnets are close, their fields combine.
bullets: **Unlike poles facing (N to S)**: lines go straight across the gap from N to S; the magnets attract.
**Like poles facing (N to N or S to S)**: the lines push away from each other and curve sideways, leaving a **neutral point** midway where the fields cancel and there is no field.
At a neutral point a compass needle does not settle in any particular direction.

callouts.p: Attracting: lines join across the gap. Repelling: lines turn away from each other and a neutral point appears.

core.p: A **plotting compass** is a small compass with a freely rotating **magnetised needle**. The needle is itself a tiny magnet, so it lines up with the field and its **north end points along the field direction** (towards the S pole of the magnet).
bullets: Shows **direction** at a point, not only shape.
Small size lets you map the field point by point.
The direction it points is the direction of the field line at that place.
Iron filings show shape quickly but **cannot show direction**, so compasses are better for direction.

core.h: Method: mapping a field with a plotting compass
core.p: This is a common 4 to 6 mark describe question.
bullets: Place the bar magnet on a sheet of paper and **draw round it**; mark N and S.
Put the plotting compass near the **north pole** of the magnet.
Mark a **pencil dot** at the point where the compass needle's **north end points**.
**Move the compass** so its tail (S end) is on that dot, and mark a new dot at the needle tip.
Repeat until you reach the **south pole**.
**Join the dots** with a smooth curve and add an **arrow** from N to S.
Repeat from different starting points to draw several field lines.
Keep other magnets and steel objects away, as they would distort the field.

callouts.p: Dot at the end of the needle; move compass so tail is on the dot; repeat; join dots; arrows N to S; repeat for other lines.

core.h: Using a compass to show the Earth's field (12.5)
core.p: Away from any magnets, a compass needle still settles pointing **north**. This shows the **Earth has its own magnetic field**.
bullets: Wherever you take a compass on Earth's surface, its N end points towards the **Earth's (magnetic) north**.
Using a compass at many places shows the field has a pattern like that of a **bar magnet**.
If the Earth had no field, the needle would point in a random direction and stay wherever it was left.
A freely suspended bar magnet behaves the same way, which is why its N pole is called north-seeking.

core.h: Evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic (12.6)
core.p: The **behaviour of a compass** is evidence that the Earth's core must be magnetic: compasses align with a field that has the **same shape as a bar magnet's field**, and the source must be inside the Earth.
bullets: Compasses everywhere point roughly north, so there is a magnetic field around the whole Earth.
The pattern matches the field of a **bar magnet** inside the Earth.
Such a large field must come from deep inside the Earth: the **core**, which contains **iron and nickel** (magnetic materials).
The N end of a compass is attracted towards geographic north, and **unlike poles attract**, so the magnetic pole near the **geographic North Pole is actually a magnetic south pole**.
The Earth's magnetic poles are close to, but not exactly at, the geographic poles.

callouts.p: Compass N end points north; unlike poles attract; so there is a magnetic SOUTH pole near the geographic North Pole.
Do not say the Earth's geographic North Pole is a magnetic north pole.

fig.cap: Figure 4: The Earth's field is like that of a bar magnet in its core. The magnet's south pole is near the geographic North Pole, so field lines run from the geographic south to the geographic north and compass needles point north.

core.p: Questions mix sketching, describing a method and explaining evidence.
bullets: Sketches: at least 3 to 4 lines, smooth curves, arrows N to S, touching the poles, never crossing, closer at poles.
Uniform field: straight, parallel, equally spaced, with arrows.
Method: include dots, moving the compass, joining dots and arrows.
Earth: link compass behaviour to a field like a bar magnet, and to a magnetic core.

callouts.p: Structured answer: what you do, what you observe, what it shows.

analogy.t: Field lines as traffic on one-way streets
analogy.p: Field lines are like one-way streets drawn on a map: traffic (the push on a north pole) always flows out of N town and into S town, streets never cross, and where the streets are packed close together (near the poles) the 'traffic' is heaviest, meaning the field is strongest. A uniform field is a set of straight, evenly spaced parallel motorway lanes. A plotting compass is a driver who always faces along the street they are on. Where it breaks down: nothing actually flows along field lines; they are only a picture of the force direction, and real fields exist everywhere between the lines too.

terms.d: Region around a magnet where another magnet or a magnetic material experiences a force.
A line showing the direction of the force on a north pole at each point; drawn from N to S.
The direction of the force that would act on a north pole placed at that point.
How strong the magnetic force is at a point; shown by how close together the field lines are.
How closely spaced the lines are; higher concentration means a stronger field.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, shown by parallel, equally spaced lines.
A small compass whose magnetised needle lines up with a magnetic field, its N end pointing along the field.
Small pieces of iron that become induced magnets and line up to show the shape (not direction) of a field.
A point where two magnetic fields cancel so the overall field is zero.
The magnetic field around the Earth, shaped like that of a bar magnet, produced in the core.
The Earth's iron and nickel core, which the evidence from compasses shows must be magnetic.
The northern end of the Earth's axis of rotation; a magnetic south pole lies near it.
The pole of a magnet or compass needle that points towards the Earth's geographic north.

mistakes.r: Outside a magnet, field lines go from the north pole to the south pole.

mistakes.r: Every line needs an arrow (N to S) and lines never cross.

mistakes.r: The field is strongest at the poles, where the lines are most concentrated.

exam.q: State the direction of magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
model: From the north pole to the south pole.
exam.tip: N to S.

exam.q: State how the strength of a magnetic field is shown on a field line diagram.
model: By how close together the lines are: closer lines mean a stronger field.
exam.tip: Use the word concentration or closeness.

exam.q: Draw the magnetic field pattern around a bar magnet.
model: At least four smooth lines from pole to pole around the magnet.
Arrows pointing from N to S.
Lines closer together near the poles and not crossing.
exam.tip: Lines must touch the poles.

exam.q: Describe a uniform magnetic field and state how one can be produced.
model: Same strength and direction everywhere / parallel, equally spaced lines.
Produced between opposite (N and S) poles facing each other.
exam.tip: Name opposite poles facing.

exam.q: Describe how a plotting compass can be used to plot the magnetic field lines around a bar magnet.
model: Place magnet on paper; put compass near N pole.
Mark a dot where the needle points (at its N end).
Move compass so its tail is at the dot; mark the next dot; repeat until reaching the S pole.
Join the dots and add arrows from N to S; repeat for other lines.
exam.tip: Four separate steps for four marks.

exam.q: Give one advantage of using a plotting compass rather than iron filings to show a magnetic field.
model: A compass shows the direction of the field as well as its shape.
exam.tip: Direction is the key word.

exam.q: A compass is held far from any magnet. Explain why the needle points north.
model: The Earth has a magnetic field.
The compass needle (a magnet) lines up with the Earth's field, its N end pointing to magnetic north.
exam.tip: Mention the Earth's field.

exam.q: Explain why the magnetic pole near the Earth's geographic North Pole is a south pole.
model: The north pole of a compass needle is attracted towards geographic north.
Unlike poles attract, so the magnetic pole there must be a south pole.
exam.tip: Use unlike poles attract.

exam.q: Explain how the behaviour of a compass provides evidence that the Earth's core is magnetic.
model: A compass needle always points (roughly) north wherever it is on Earth.
So the Earth has a magnetic field.
The field pattern is like that of a bar magnet.
This field must come from inside the Earth, so the core (iron/nickel) must be magnetic.
exam.tip: Chain: compass behaviour, field exists, bar-magnet shape, source in core.

exam.q: Two bar magnets are placed with their north poles facing each other. Describe the field pattern between them.
model: Field lines curve away from each other / do not join across the gap.
There is a neutral point midway between the poles where there is no field.
exam.tip: Like poles: lines turn away.

worked.q: Model answer: Describe how to show the shape and direction of the field around a bar magnet using a plotting compass (6 marks).
steps: Place the bar magnet in the middle of a sheet of paper and draw round it, labelling N and S.
Place a plotting compass next to the north pole.
Mark a pencil dot at the position of the north end of the compass needle.
Move the compass so that the south end (tail) of the needle is on the dot, then mark a new dot at the north end.
Repeat until the compass reaches the south pole, then join the dots with a smooth curve.
Draw an arrow on the line in the direction the compass needle pointed (N to S), and repeat from other starting points to build up the full pattern.
worked.ans: A set of smooth curves from N to S, closer together near the poles, each with an arrow from N to S.

worked.q: A diagram shows field lines 2 mm apart at point A near a pole and 8 mm apart at point B further away. A plotting compass is placed at each. Compare the field at A and B.
steps: Closer lines mean a more concentrated field, so A has the stronger field.
Lines at A are 4 times closer, so the field at A is much stronger than at B.
At both points the compass needle's N end lines up along the field line, pointing in the field direction (towards the S pole).
worked.ans: Field at A is stronger than at B; at each point the compass points along the field line from N towards S.

phy_edx.11.2.summary: A **current in a wire produces a magnetic field**: around a **long straight conductor** the field lines are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, with their direction given by the **right-hand grip rule** and reversed if the current is reversed. The field is **stronger for a larger current** and **weaker further from the wire**. Coiling the wire into a **solenoid** makes the fields of the individual turns **add together inside** to give a **strong, almost uniform field along the centre**, while they **cancel outside** to give a **weaker field**, so the solenoid's outside field looks like a bar magnet's.

core.h: Electric current creates a magnetic effect
core.p: Any wire carrying an electric current is surrounded by a **magnetic field**. This is the basis of electromagnets, motors and loudspeakers. Switch the current off and the field disappears.
bullets: Magnetism caused by an electric current is called **electromagnetism**.
The field exists only **while current flows**.
The **bigger the current**, the stronger the field.
Reversing the current **reverses the field direction**.

callouts.p: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field around it.

core.h: Showing the magnetic effect of a straight wire (12.7)
core.p: To **show** that a current creates a magnetic effect, pass a long straight wire **vertically through a horizontal piece of card** and connect it to a d.c. supply.
bullets: Place **plotting compasses** on the card around the wire, or sprinkle **iron filings** and tap the card gently.
Switch the current **on**: the compasses turn to point around the wire in circles / the filings form **concentric circles**.
Switch **off**: compasses swing back to point north (the Earth's field).
**Reverse the current**: the compass needles **reverse direction**, showing the field direction depends on current direction.
Use a **large current** (low resistance wire), switched on only briefly, because the field of a straight wire is weak and the wire gets hot.

callouts.p: Switch off between readings: a large current heats the wire. Keep other magnets away so they do not affect the compasses.

core.h: Shape of the field round a straight wire
core.p: The field lines around a long straight conductor are **concentric circles** centred on the wire, lying in a plane **at right angles (perpendicular) to the wire**.
bullets: Circles get **further apart** with distance from the wire, showing the field gets **weaker**.
There are **no poles**: the lines are closed loops with no start or end.
Viewed end-on, current into the page is drawn as a **cross** (the tail of an arrow); current out of the page is a **dot** (the tip of an arrow).

callouts.p: Concentric circles centred on the wire, in a plane perpendicular to it; direction given by the right-hand grip rule.

core.p: Edexcel asks you to **relate the direction of the magnetic field to the direction of the current**. Use the **right-hand grip rule**.
bullets: Grip the wire with your **right hand**, **thumb pointing in the direction of the (conventional) current**.
Your **curled fingers** show the **direction of the magnetic field lines**.
Current into page: **clockwise** field. Current out of page: **anticlockwise** field.
Reverse the current and the field direction reverses.
Conventional current flows from + to - around the circuit.

head: Current direction
Field direction (viewed from where current comes towards you or away)

callouts.p: Use your RIGHT hand. Left hand is for Fleming's left-hand rule (motor effect), a different rule.

core.h: What the field strength depends on (12.8)
core.p: You must **recall** that the strength of the field around a long straight conductor depends on **the size of the current** and **the distance from the conductor**.
bullets: **Larger current** gives a **stronger field**.
**Greater distance** from the wire gives a **weaker field**.
On a diagram: lines are closer together near the wire and further apart further away.
More current: draw the circles closer together overall.
Practical test: a compass further from the wire is deflected less; doubling the current deflects compasses more strongly.

head: Change
Effect on field strength
rows: No change in strength; direction reverses

callouts.p: Field strength increases with current and decreases with distance from the wire.

core.p: A **solenoid** is a long coil of wire, an example of a coil. Each turn of the coil carries the same current and so produces its own circular field.
bullets: Wrapping the wire into many turns lets the fields of each turn **combine**.
The turns are close together, so neighbouring fields reinforce each other.
A solenoid with a **soft iron core** is an **electromagnet**.

callouts.p: A long coil of wire; when current flows, it produces a strong, almost uniform field inside and a bar-magnet-shaped field outside.

core.p: Inside the solenoid, the fields from all the individual turns **point in the same direction**, so they **add together** to form a **very strong, almost uniform field along the centre** of the solenoid.
bullets: Lines inside are **straight, parallel and close together** (strong and uniform).
Field direction inside runs from the **S end to the N end** of the solenoid.
Every turn adds its field, so **more turns** give a stronger field.
The field is weaker and less uniform near the very ends.

callouts.p: The fields from individual turns are in the same direction inside, so they add together.

core.p: Outside the solenoid, the fields from turns on opposite sides of the coil point in **opposite directions**, so they largely **cancel**, giving a **weaker field outside**.
bullets: Lines outside are **spread out**, showing a weaker field.
The outside field pattern is the **same shape as a bar magnet's field**.
One end acts as a **north pole**, the other as a **south pole**.
Lines leave the N end, loop round outside, and enter the S end, then continue through the inside back to N: closed loops.

callouts.p: Inside the solenoid the field runs S to N; outside it runs N to S. Lines are continuous loops.

core.h: Finding the poles of a solenoid
core.p: Use the right-hand grip rule a second way: **curl your fingers in the direction of the current in the turns**; your **thumb points to the north pole** end.
bullets: Alternatively look at an end: current **anticlockwise** = **N pole**; current **clockwise** = **S pole**.
Reverse the current and the poles swap.
A compass near the N end has its S end attracted towards the solenoid.

callouts.p: Draw an N with arrows on its ends (anticlockwise) and an S with arrows (clockwise) to remember end-view polarity.

core.p: Linking ideas: anything that increases the field from each turn or the number of turns adding together makes the solenoid stronger.
bullets: **Increase the current**.
**Increase the number of turns** (for the same length).
Add a **soft iron core**: it becomes an **induced magnet** and greatly increases the field. This makes an **electromagnet**.
Soft iron is used because it loses its magnetism when the current is switched off, so the electromagnet can be turned off.

core.p: Compare the two patterns, as exam questions often ask you to.
bullets: Wire: circles, no poles, field weakens with distance.
Solenoid: uniform field inside, bar-magnet field outside, has N and S poles.
Both: field direction reverses when current reverses, strength increases with current.

core.p: Questions ask you to draw patterns, describe the card experiment and explain the solenoid field.
bullets: Wire diagram: at least 3 concentric circles, spacing increasing outwards, arrows consistent with the current.
Solenoid: straight parallel lines inside, curved lines outside, arrows S to N inside and N to S outside.
Explain: use the words **add together** (inside) and **cancel** (outside).
Recall factors: current and distance (wire).

callouts.p: Examiners often give a mark for circles getting further apart further from the wire.

analogy.p: Current through a wire is like water swirling down a plughole: the water circles round the drain in rings, swirling fastest close to the drain (strong field near the wire) and more gently further out (weaker field). Pull the plug harder (more current) and the swirl is stronger; reverse the flow and the swirl reverses. A solenoid is like a row of many drains side by side all swirling the same way: between them the swirls point the same way along the middle and add up to a strong steady stream, while on the outside they partly cancel. Where it breaks down: a magnetic field is not a flow of anything, and water swirls are not exactly circular or perpendicular in the same way.

terms.d: The magnetic effect produced by an electric current.
A straight current-carrying wire whose field is concentric circles around it.
Circles of different sizes sharing the same centre; the field pattern around a straight wire.
Grip the wire with the right hand, thumb along the current; fingers curl in the direction of the magnetic field.
Current direction taken as from the positive to the negative terminal of the supply.
A long coil of wire that produces a magnetic field when a current flows through it.
A wire wound into a series of turns or loops.
A field with the same strength and direction at all points; found along the centre of a solenoid.
When fields point in the same direction they combine to make a stronger field, as inside a solenoid.
When fields point in opposite directions they combine to make a weaker field, as outside a solenoid.
A solenoid with a soft iron core; a magnet that can be switched on and off.
Iron inside a coil that becomes an induced magnet and increases the field strength; loses magnetism when current stops.
Small compass used to show the direction of the field around a wire or solenoid.
Cross = current into the page; dot = current out of the page.

exam.q: State the shape of the magnetic field around a long straight current-carrying wire.
model: Concentric circles (centred on the wire).
exam.tip: Say concentric and centred on the wire.

exam.q: State two factors that affect the strength of the magnetic field around a long straight conductor.
model: Size of the current.
Distance from the wire.
exam.tip: Exactly the two from the spec.

exam.q: Describe how the field changes as you move further from a current-carrying wire.
model: It gets weaker (lines further apart).
exam.tip: Link to spacing.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to show that a current in a long straight wire produces a magnetic field.
model: Pass the wire vertically through a horizontal card.
Place plotting compasses (or iron filings) on the card around the wire.
Switch the current on: compasses point in a circle around the wire / filings form circles.
Reverse the current: compass needles reverse, showing direction depends on current.
exam.tip: Include an observation and what it shows.

exam.q: The current in a wire flows into the page. State the direction of the field lines around it and the rule used.
model: Clockwise.
Right-hand grip rule (thumb in direction of current, fingers show field).
exam.tip: Into = clockwise.

exam.q: State what happens to the compass needles around a wire when the current is reversed.
model: They point in the opposite direction (field reverses).
exam.tip: Direction reverses; strength unchanged.

exam.q: Draw the magnetic field pattern inside and outside a solenoid.
model: Straight, parallel, equally spaced lines inside the solenoid.
Lines outside curve from one end to the other like a bar magnet.
Arrows consistent: S to N inside, N to S outside.
exam.tip: Lines are continuous loops.

exam.q: Explain why the magnetic field inside a solenoid is strong and almost uniform.
model: The fields from each turn (coil) point in the same direction inside.
So they add together to give a strong, (almost) uniform field.
exam.tip: Use 'add together'.

exam.q: Explain why the magnetic field outside a solenoid is weaker than inside.
model: Outside, the fields from the individual turns are in opposite directions.
So they (partly) cancel, giving a weaker field.
exam.tip: Use 'cancel'.

exam.q: Explain the magnetic field patterns produced by a current in a long straight wire and in a solenoid. Include how the strength of each field can be changed.
model: Wire: concentric circles centred on the wire, perpendicular to it.
Direction given by right-hand grip rule; reverses if current reverses.
Wire field is stronger with larger current and weaker further from the wire.
Solenoid: fields of individual turns add together inside to give a strong, almost uniform field.
Outside, the fields cancel to give a weaker field with a bar-magnet shape, with N and S poles.
Solenoid field stronger with larger current, more turns or a soft iron core.
exam.tip: Cover both shapes, direction and strength.

worked.q: Two plotting compasses P and Q are placed 2 cm and 6 cm from a vertical wire carrying an upward current. The current is then doubled. Describe what the compasses show before and after.
steps: The field lines are circles centred on the wire, so each compass points at a tangent to a circle around the wire.
Current upwards: by the right-hand grip rule the field is anticlockwise when viewed from above, so both compasses point anticlockwise around the wire.
P is closer, so the field at P is stronger; Q is further away, so its field is weaker and the Earth's field affects Q more.
Doubling the current makes the field stronger at both points, so both compasses line up more closely around the wire; the direction does not change.
worked.ans: Both point anticlockwise (viewed from above) around the wire; P feels a stronger field than Q; doubling the current strengthens both fields without changing direction.

worked.q: Looking at the right-hand end of a solenoid, the current in the turns flows anticlockwise. State which pole this end is, the direction of the field inside, and what happens if the current is reversed.
steps: Current anticlockwise when viewed from an end means that end is a north pole.
Inside a solenoid the field runs from the S end to the N end, so inside the field points towards the right-hand end.
Outside, field lines leave the right-hand (N) end and loop round to the left-hand (S) end.
Reversing the current swaps the poles: the right-hand end becomes a south pole and all field directions reverse.
worked.ans: Right-hand end is N; field inside points towards it (left to right); reversing the current makes it a S pole and reverses the field.

phy_edx.11.3.summary: When a wire carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field (for example between the poles of a magnet) it experiences a force: this is the **motor effect**. The force happens because the magnetic field around the current-carrying wire **interacts** with the field of the magnet, and by Newton's third law the magnet feels an **equal and opposite force**. When the current and the field are at right angles, **Fleming's left-hand rule** gives the direction of the force, which reverses if either the current or the field is reversed.

core.p: A conductor (usually a wire) carrying an electric current, placed in a magnetic field, has a **force** exerted on it. If the wire is free to move, it moves. This is called the **motor effect** because it is the basic idea behind every electric motor.
bullets: You need **both** a current in the conductor **and** an external magnetic field (e.g. from a permanent magnet or electromagnet).
No current means no force: an ordinary copper wire is not magnetic and is not attracted to a magnet.
The force is largest when the wire is at **right angles (perpendicular)** to the magnetic field lines.
There is **no force** when the wire is **parallel** to the field lines.
Reversing the current, or reversing the field, **reverses the direction** of the force.

A classic demonstration: a short metal rod resting on two horizontal metal rails between the poles of a magnet rolls along the rails when a current is switched on (the 'catapult' or 'rail' experiment).

callouts.p: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force. This is called the motor effect.

core.h: Why there is a force: interacting magnetic fields
core.p: A current in a wire creates its **own magnetic field**: circles around the wire. When the wire is in the field of a magnet, the two fields **interact** (combine). The force on the wire is a result of this **interaction between the two magnetic fields**, in the same way that two magnets push or pull on each other.
bullets: The field around a straight wire is a set of **concentric circles**; its direction is found with the right-hand grip rule (thumb along current, fingers curl the way the field goes).
On one side of the wire the wire's field points the **same way** as the magnet's field, so they **add**: the combined field is **stronger** (field lines closer together).
On the other side the two fields point in **opposite** directions, so they partly **cancel**: the combined field is **weaker**.
The wire is pushed **from the stronger field towards the weaker field**, like a stretched catapult elastic: this is sometimes called the **catapult field**.
This is why the force is at **right angles** to the field: the strong and weak regions are above and below the wire, not in front and behind it.
The bigger the current, the stronger the wire's own field, so the stronger the interaction and the bigger the force.

callouts.p: The force is due to the **interaction** between the magnetic field of the magnet and the magnetic field produced by the current in the wire.

core.h: Equal and opposite force on the magnet
core.p: Forces always come in **Newton's third law pairs**. If the magnet pushes on the wire, the wire pushes back on the magnet with a force that is **equal in size and opposite in direction**.
bullets: The two forces act on **different objects**: one on the wire, one on the magnet.
Both forces are **magnetic forces** (same type of force), as a third-law pair must be.

Demonstration: put a magnet on a **top-pan balance** and clamp a wire through its field so the wire cannot move. Switching on the current changes the balance reading, because the wire now pushes up or down on the magnet.
If the wire is pushed upwards, the magnet is pushed downwards by the same amount (the balance reading goes up), and vice versa.
If the magnet were free to move and the wire were fixed, it would be the **magnet** that moved.

callouts.p: A current-carrying conductor near a magnet experiences a force, and the magnet experiences an **equal and opposite force**.
The two forces do not cancel out, because they act on different objects. Only forces on the same object can balance.

core.p: When the current and the magnetic field are **mutually perpendicular** (all at right angles to each other), **Fleming's left-hand rule** shows the relative directions of the **force**, the **current** and the **magnetic field**. Hold your **left** hand with the thumb, first finger and second finger all at right angles to one another.
bullets: **thuMb** = **Motion** (direction of the **force** on the conductor).
**First finger** = **Field** (direction of the magnetic field, from **north to south**).
**seCond finger** = **Current** (direction of **conventional current**, from **positive to negative**).
Method: point the First finger along the field (N to S), turn your hand until the seCond finger points along the current, then read the force from the thuMb.
Use your **LEFT** hand for the motor effect (force on a current). The right hand is used for other rules, so using it gives the opposite answer.
The rule only works directly when field and current are at right angles; GCSE questions only use this case.

callouts.t: Say it as you do it
callouts.p: In the exam physically use your left hand and say 'Field, Current, Motion' while you line up each finger. Students who do it in their head often get it backwards.

core.p: Exam diagrams often show a wire end-on, pointing into or out of the paper. You must read these symbols to use Fleming's rule.
bullets: **Cross (x)** = current going **into** the page (like seeing the flights on the back of a dart moving away from you).
**Dot** = current coming **out of** the page (like seeing the point of a dart coming towards you).
Magnetic field lines between magnets always go from the **N pole to the S pole**.
Conventional current flows from the **positive (+) terminal** of the cell round the circuit to the **negative (-) terminal**; the long line on a cell symbol is positive.
For a field left to right and current into the page, the force is **downwards**; current out of the page gives a force **upwards**.

callouts.p: Fleming's rule uses conventional current (+ to -). Electrons move the opposite way, so using electron flow gives the wrong force direction.

core.h: Reversing the direction of the force
core.p: The force direction depends on the directions of both the current and the field. Change one and the force flips; change both and the force stays the same.
bullets: **Reverse the current** (swap the connections to the power supply): force reverses.
**Reverse the magnetic field** (turn the magnet round / swap the poles): force reverses.
**Reverse both** current and field: the two changes cancel and the force is in the **original** direction.
Changing the **size** of the current or field changes the **size** of the force, not its direction.
This is why an alternating current (a.c.) in a wire in a fixed field produces a force that keeps changing direction, making the wire vibrate (used in loudspeakers).

core.h: What affects the size of the force
core.p: Although the calculation belongs to the next spec point, you should already be able to say qualitatively what makes the motor-effect force bigger.
bullets: A **larger current** in the wire gives a larger force.
A **stronger magnetic field** (stronger magnet, poles closer together) gives a larger force.
A **longer length of wire inside the field** gives a larger force (more of the wire is being pushed).
The **angle** matters: maximum force when the wire is perpendicular to the field, zero when parallel.
Coiling the wire so several lengths pass through the field (all with current the same way) multiplies the force.

callouts.p: Say 'increase the current' or 'use a stronger magnet', not 'more power' or 'bigger magnet'. A bigger magnet is not necessarily a stronger one.

core.p: A light metal rod rests across two parallel horizontal metal rails connected to a d.c. supply, with a horseshoe magnet placed so the field is vertical through the rod. Exam questions ask you to predict and explain what happens.
bullets: When the switch is closed, current flows through the rod, which is at right angles to the vertical field.
The field of the current interacts with the field of the magnet, producing a force on the rod.
The force is horizontal and along the rails (at right angles to both the rod and the field), so the rod **rolls along the rails**.
Direction is found with Fleming's left-hand rule; reversing the supply or turning the magnet over makes it roll the other way.
A bigger current makes it accelerate faster (bigger force, F = ma).
If the rod rolls off the end of the magnet's field, the force stops.

core.p: The motor effect does not need a permanent magnet: any magnetic field will do, including the field of another current. This is a good test of the 'interacting fields' idea.
bullets: Each wire sits in the magnetic field produced by the other wire, so each experiences a force.
Two parallel wires carrying currents in the **same direction** attract; in **opposite directions** they repel.
The forces on the two wires are equal and opposite (Newton's third law again).

callouts.p: Magnetic forces between any two objects (magnets or currents) are due to the interaction of their magnetic fields.

core.h: Linking to motors and other devices
core.p: The motor effect turns electrical energy into kinetic energy. Devices that use it put a coil of wire in a magnetic field.
bullets: In a **d.c. motor**, the two sides of a coil carry current in opposite directions, so the forces on them are in opposite directions and the coil turns (covered in 12.14P).
In a **loudspeaker**, a.c. in a coil in a magnetic field makes the coil and cone move back and forth, producing sound waves.
Energy transfer: electrical work done by the supply becomes kinetic energy of the moving wire (plus some wasted thermal energy from the wire's resistance).

core.p: Marks come from a clear chain of cause and effect. A strong answer to 'Explain why the wire moves' uses this structure.
bullets: 1. There is a **current** in the wire, so it produces its **own magnetic field** around it.
2. This field **interacts** with the field of the **permanent magnet**.
3. This produces a **force** on the wire (the **motor effect**).
4. The force is at right angles to the current and the field; its direction is given by **Fleming's left-hand rule**.
5. If asked about the magnet: an **equal and opposite** force acts on the magnet.

callouts.p: Never say the wire is 'attracted to the magnet'. The force is sideways (perpendicular to the field), not towards a pole.

analogy.t: A finger flicking a stretched elastic band (the catapult)
analogy.p: Imagine the magnet's field lines as stretched elastic bands running from N to S. The current-carrying wire bends the bands: on one side they bunch up and are stretched tighter (stronger field), on the other side they go slack (weaker field). Like a catapult, the tight bands fling the wire towards the slack side, so the force is sideways across the field lines. Where it breaks down: field lines are not real objects and do not store energy like rubber, and there is nothing 'pulled back' before the current is switched on; the force exists only while the current flows and appears instantly.

terms.d: The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field.
A material (such as a copper wire) that allows an electric current to flow through it.
The region around a magnet or current-carrying conductor where a magnetic material or another magnet/current experiences a force.
The direction a north pole would be pushed; field lines go from north to south outside a magnet.
The direction of current used in rules and diagrams: from the positive terminal to the negative terminal, opposite to electron flow.
The combining of the field of the magnet with the field of the current; where they add the field is stronger, where they oppose it is weaker, producing a force.
The combined, distorted field around a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field, which pushes the wire from the stronger region to the weaker region.
A rule using the left hand (thumb, first and second fingers at right angles) to give the relative directions of force (thumb), field (first finger) and current (second finger).
All at right angles to each other, like the three edges meeting at the corner of a box.
When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
The force exerted by the wire on the magnet: the same size as the force on the wire but in the opposite direction.
Shows a current flowing into the page in an end-on view of a wire.
Shows a current flowing out of the page in an end-on view of a wire.
Thumb of the right hand along the current; the curled fingers show the direction of the circular magnetic field around the wire.
A magnet that produces its own magnetic field all the time, used as the external field in motor-effect experiments.

mistakes.w: The wire is attracted towards the north pole of the magnet.
mistakes.r: The force is at right angles to the field (and the current), not towards either pole.

mistakes.w: Uses the right hand for the motor effect.
mistakes.r: Fleming's LEFT-hand rule for the force on a current-carrying conductor.

mistakes.w: Uses the direction of electron flow as the current.
mistakes.r: Use conventional current, from positive to negative.

mistakes.w: Draws or reads the field from S to N.
mistakes.r: Magnetic field lines go from north to south.

mistakes.w: The force is caused by the magnet attracting the copper wire.
mistakes.r: The force is due to the interaction between the magnet's field and the field produced by the current in the wire.

mistakes.w: Reversing both the current and the magnet reverses the force.
mistakes.r: Reversing both leaves the force in the same direction; reversing just one reverses it.

mistakes.w: There is no force on the magnet because the magnet is not carrying a current.
mistakes.r: An equal and opposite force acts on the magnet (Newton's third law).

mistakes.w: The wire and the magnet forces cancel out, so nothing moves.
mistakes.r: The forces act on different objects so they cannot cancel; each object can move.

mistakes.w: A wire parallel to the field lines has the biggest force.
mistakes.r: A wire parallel to the field has no force; the force is greatest at right angles.

exam.q: State the name given to the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
model: The motor effect.
exam.tip: Two words; spell 'motor effect' exactly.

exam.q: In Fleming's left-hand rule, what does the second finger represent?
model: The (conventional) current.
exam.tip: seCond = Current.

exam.q: A wire carries a current into the page. The magnetic field is from left to right across the page. State the direction of the force on the wire.
model: Downwards (towards the bottom of the page).
exam.tip: First finger right, second finger into page, thumb points down.

exam.q: Give two ways of reversing the direction of the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field.
model: Reverse the direction of the current (swap the connections to the supply).
Reverse the magnetic field (turn the magnet round / swap the poles).
exam.tip: Do not say 'reverse both' - that leaves the force unchanged.

exam.q: A wire is placed between the poles of a magnet, first parallel to the field and then perpendicular to it, with the same current. Compare the forces.
model: Parallel to the field: no force (zero).
Perpendicular to the field: maximum force.
exam.tip: Give both cases explicitly.

exam.q: A magnet sits on a top-pan balance. A fixed wire passes through its field. When the current is switched on, the force on the wire is upwards. Explain what happens to the balance reading.
model: By Newton's third law an equal and opposite (downwards) force acts on the magnet.
So the balance reading increases.
exam.tip: Link to Newton's third law by name for the explanation mark.

exam.q: Explain why a current-carrying wire placed between the poles of a magnet experiences a force.
model: The current produces a magnetic field around the wire.
This field interacts with the field of the magnet, producing a force.
exam.tip: 'Interacts' is the key word.

exam.q: Describe how the combined magnetic field around a current-carrying wire in a uniform magnetic field explains the direction of the force on the wire.
model: The wire produces a circular magnetic field around it.
On one side the wire's field is in the same direction as the magnet's field, so the fields add / the field is stronger.
On the other side they are in opposite directions, so they (partly) cancel / the field is weaker.
The wire is pushed from the stronger field towards the weaker field (at right angles to the field).
exam.tip: Say which side is strong and which is weak, then give the direction.

exam.q: A metal rod rests on two horizontal metal rails connected to a battery and switch. A magnet provides a vertical field through the rod. Explain what happens when the switch is closed and how the rod's motion could be made to accelerate more quickly and move in the opposite direction.
model: A current flows in the rod and the rod experiences a force (motor effect) along the rails.
So the rod rolls along the rails.
A larger current / stronger magnet gives a bigger force and so a larger acceleration.
Reversing the current or the field makes the rod roll the opposite way.
exam.tip: Each instruction in the question earns its own mark - cover all three.

exam.q: Explain, in terms of magnetic fields and forces, what happens when a wire carrying a current is placed at right angles to the field between the poles of a permanent magnet. Include how the directions of the force can be found and what happens to the magnet.
model: A current in the wire produces a magnetic field (concentric circles) around the wire.
This field interacts with the magnetic field of the permanent magnet.
The result is a force on the wire (the motor effect), so the wire moves if free.
The force is at right angles to both the current and the magnetic field.
The direction is found with Fleming's left-hand rule: first finger field (N to S), second finger current, thumb force/motion.
An equal and opposite force acts on the magnet (Newton's third law); reversing current or field reverses the force.
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need a logical sequence: cause (current/field), mechanism (interaction), effect (force), direction (rule), consequence (magnet). Use the key words.

worked.q: A horizontal wire runs from west to east and carries a current from west to east. It is in a magnetic field pointing vertically downwards. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to find the direction of the force.
steps: Point the First finger of your left hand along the field: straight down.
Rotate your hand so the seCond finger points along the current: east.
Your thuMb now points north.
Check: the force is at right angles to both the field (vertical) and the current (east-west).
worked.ans: The force on the wire is horizontal, towards the north.

worked.q: A wire shown end-on with a dot (current out of the page) is placed in a field that runs from top to bottom of the page. Find the direction of the force, then say what happens if the magnet is turned round and the current is also reversed.
steps: First finger of the left hand: along the field, down the page.
seCond finger: along the current, out of the page towards you.
Hold your hand so both line up: the thuMb now points to the right of the page.
Turning the magnet round reverses the field, which on its own would reverse the force (to the left).
Also reversing the current reverses the force again, back to the right: two reversals cancel.
worked.ans: The force is to the right. With both the field and the current reversed the force is still to the right.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why the magnet in a motor-effect experiment also experiences a force.
steps: Identify the pair: the magnet exerts a force on the wire.
Apply Newton's third law: the wire exerts a force on the magnet.
State size and direction: equal in size, opposite in direction.
State type and object: both are magnetic forces, acting on different objects.
worked.ans: Because the magnet exerts a force on the current-carrying wire, by Newton's third law the wire exerts an equal and opposite (magnetic) force on the magnet.

phy_edx.11.4.summary: The size of the motor-effect force on a straight wire at right angles to a magnetic field is given by **F = B x I x l**: force (N) = magnetic flux density (T) x current (A) x length of wire in the field (m). The force is **directly proportional** to each of these three quantities, is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field and is **zero** when the wire is parallel to it. This is Higher tier content: you must be able to select the equation from the equation sheet, rearrange it, convert units and explain what each term means, including the unit **tesla (T)**.

core.p: For a straight conductor carrying a current **at right angles to a magnetic field**, the force on it is the product of the field strength, the current and the length of conductor inside the field.
bullets: **F = B x I x l** (often written F = BIl).
**F** = force on the conductor, in **newtons (N)**.
**B** = **magnetic flux density** (the strength of the magnetic field), in **tesla (T)**, which is the same as **N/A m** (newtons per amp per metre).
**I** = current in the conductor, in **amperes (A)**.
**l** = **length of conductor in the field**, in **metres (m)**.
The equation is on the Edexcel equation sheet; your job is to choose it, substitute correctly and give units.

head: Symbol
Quantity
Unit
rows: Length of conductor in the field

callouts.p: Force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field carrying a current = magnetic flux density x current x length.

core.h: Magnetic flux density and the tesla
core.p: **Magnetic flux density**, B, measures **how strong** a magnetic field is: you can picture it as how closely packed the field lines are. A bigger B means a bigger force on the same wire with the same current.
bullets: Rearranging gives **B = F / (I x l)**: B is the force per unit current per unit length of wire.
So **1 tesla** is the flux density that produces a force of **1 N** on **1 m** of wire carrying **1 A** at right angles to the field.
That is why the tesla can be written **N/A m** (sometimes N A^-1 m^-1).
1 T is a strong field. School magnets are typically around 0.01 T to 0.5 T; the Earth's field is only about 0.00005 T (50 microtesla).
Small fields are often given in **millitesla (mT)**: 1 mT = 0.001 T. Convert before calculating.

callouts.p: The unit of magnetic flux density is the **tesla (T)**. Do not write 'Tesla units' or 'teslas per metre'.

core.p: Questions often give the force and ask for the current, the length or the flux density. Rearrange before substituting.
bullets: **F = B x I x l**
Formula triangle: F on top, B, I and l along the bottom; cover the quantity you want.
Always write the equation, substitute numbers with units, then give the answer with a unit (each can be a mark).

callouts.p: In a 3-mark calculation you usually get a mark for substitution even if your final answer is wrong, so always write the numbers into the equation.

core.h: Unit conversions that catch students out
core.p: The equation only works with N, T, A and m. Exam questions deliberately give values in other units.
bullets: Length in **cm**: divide by 100 (e.g. 8.0 cm = 0.080 m).
Length in **mm**: divide by 1000 (e.g. 25 mm = 0.025 m).
Current in **mA**: divide by 1000 (e.g. 250 mA = 0.25 A).
Flux density in **mT**: divide by 1000 (e.g. 40 mT = 0.040 T).
Force in **mN**: 1 mN = 0.001 N.
Check the size of your answer: forces in school experiments are usually a few hundredths of a newton.

callouts.p: Forgetting to convert centimetres to metres makes the answer 100 times too big.

core.p: Because F is the product B x I x l, the force is **directly proportional** to each quantity while the other two are kept constant.
bullets: Double the current: the force doubles.
Double the flux density: the force doubles.
Double the length of wire in the field: the force doubles.
Double the current and halve the length: the force stays the same.
A graph of F against I (B and l constant) is a **straight line through the origin**; its **gradient = B x l**.
So from such a graph you can find B: B = gradient / l.

callouts.p: For full marks on 'describe the relationship', say 'directly proportional' and refer to a straight line through the origin.

core.h: Why only the length in the field counts
core.p: The force acts only on the parts of the wire that are actually inside the magnetic field, because only there do the two fields interact.
bullets: Wire outside the poles (leads to the power supply) is in a very weak field and feels almost no force.
So l is the **length of conductor inside the field**, not the total length of the wire.
Using wider magnets (pole pieces) increases l and so increases the force.
In a coil, each turn passes through the field, so n turns side by side act like n wires: force on that side = n x B x I x l.

core.h: The angle between the wire and the field
core.p: F = BIl is for a wire **at right angles** to the field. The force depends on the angle between the wire and the field lines.
bullets: At **90 degrees** (perpendicular): **maximum** force, F = BIl.
**Parallel** to the field (0 degrees): **no force**, F = 0.
At angles in between, the force is between zero and the maximum.
This is why motor coils produce the biggest turning effect when their sides cut straight across the field.

callouts.p: If a question shows the wire along the field lines, the answer is zero force; do not calculate BIl.

core.h: Direction still comes from Fleming's left-hand rule
core.p: F = BIl gives the **size** of the force. Its **direction** is at right angles to both the current and the field and is found using Fleming's left-hand rule.
bullets: First finger = Field, seCond finger = Current, thuMb = Motion (force).
Changing the size of B, I or l changes the size of F but not its direction.
Reversing I or B reverses the direction of F but not its size.
A full answer to 'calculate the force and state its direction' needs both the number and the rule.

core.h: Measuring the force: the top-pan balance method
core.p: A common practical way to measure the motor-effect force and test F = BIl uses a magnet on a top-pan balance and a wire held still by a clamp.
bullets: Place a magnet (e.g. a U-shaped magnet or two magnets on a steel yoke) on a top-pan balance and zero the balance.
Clamp a straight wire so it passes between the poles at right angles to the field and **cannot move**.
Connect the wire in series with a power supply, ammeter and variable resistor.
Switch on: the wire exerts an **equal and opposite force on the magnet** (Newton's third law), so the balance reading changes.
Force = change in mass (in kg) x g, with **g = 10 N/kg**. For example, 2.0 g change means F = 0.0020 kg x 10 N/kg = 0.020 N.
Vary the current with the variable resistor, record the balance change each time, and plot F against I. Keep the magnet and length the same (control variables).
Switch off between readings so the wire does not get hot (resistance changes and it is a burn risk).

callouts.p: The balance measures the force on the magnet, which equals the force on the wire because they are a Newton's third law pair.
