core.p: Designers of motors, loudspeakers and other devices use F = BIl to decide how to make the force bigger.
bullets: **Increase the current** (bigger p.d. or lower resistance).
**Use a stronger magnet** (bigger B), e.g. a neodymium magnet or an electromagnet with an iron core.
**Increase the length of wire in the field**, e.g. use more turns on the coil.
Keep the wire **perpendicular** to the field.
Limits: large currents cause heating in the wire (energy wasted, insulation can melt).

core.h: Linking F = BIl to F = ma and energy
core.p: Grade 9 questions sometimes combine F = BIl with other equations.
bullets: If the wire (or rod on rails) is free to move, the force gives it an **acceleration**: a = F / m.
Example: F = 0.030 N on a rod of mass 0.015 kg gives a = 0.030 / 0.015 = 2.0 m/s^2.
Work done by the force = F x distance moved, which becomes kinetic energy of the rod (ignoring friction).
If the current is supplied from a fixed p.d., I = V / R can be used to find the current first.

analogy.p: Think of the wire as a sail and the magnetic field as the wind. A stronger wind (bigger B) pushes harder; a bigger sail across the wind (longer l in the field) catches more push; and the current I is like how much the sail is unfurled - no current, no sail, no push. If the sail is turned edge-on to the wind (wire parallel to the field) there is almost no push. Where it breaks down: wind pushes a sail in the direction the wind blows, but the magnetic force is at right angles to the field, and its direction also depends on the direction of the current.

terms.d: Force on a conductor at right angles to a magnetic field = magnetic flux density x current x length of conductor in the field.
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, equal to the force per unit current per unit length on a conductor at right angles to the field; unit tesla.
The unit of magnetic flux density; 1 T gives a force of 1 N on 1 m of wire carrying 1 A at right angles to the field (1 T = 1 N/A m).
One thousandth of a tesla: 1 mT = 0.001 T.
The rate of flow of charge, measured in amperes (A).
The length of conductor that lies inside the magnetic field, measured in metres.
The unit of force.
Two quantities are directly proportional if doubling one doubles the other; the graph is a straight line through the origin.
At right angles (90 degrees); the condition for F = BIl and for the maximum force.
Running in the same direction as the field lines; a wire parallel to the field experiences no force.
The slope of a graph; for F against I with B and l constant, gradient = B x l.
A variable kept constant in an investigation so it does not affect the result, e.g. B and l when testing how F depends on I.
Force per kilogram due to gravity; 10 N/kg is used to convert a balance mass change into a force.
Gives the direction of the force (thumb) from the field (first finger) and current (second finger).

mistakes.w: Uses the whole length of the wire, including the leads, as l.
mistakes.r: Use only the length of conductor inside the magnetic field.

mistakes.w: Substitutes a length in cm straight into F = BIl.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres first (divide cm by 100).

mistakes.w: Gives the unit of B as 'Wb', 'gauss' or 'T/m'.
mistakes.r: Tesla, T (or N/A m).

mistakes.w: Rearranges to I = F x B x l or I = B / (F l).
mistakes.r: I = F / (B x l).

mistakes.w: Calculates F = BIl for a wire parallel to the field.
mistakes.r: A wire parallel to the field experiences zero force.

mistakes.w: Says F 'increases with' the current.
mistakes.r: F is directly proportional to I (straight line through the origin) when B and l are constant.

mistakes.w: Uses the balance reading in grams as the force in newtons.
mistakes.r: Convert grams to kg, then force = mass change x 10 N/kg.

mistakes.w: Says doubling the current doubles the force and reverses its direction.
mistakes.r: Changing the size of the current only changes the size of the force; reversing the current reverses the direction.

mistakes.w: Forgets to convert mT or mA.
mistakes.r: Divide by 1000 to get T or A before substituting.

exam.q: State the unit of magnetic flux density.
model: Tesla (T) / N/A m.
exam.tip: Either form is accepted; don't invent others.

exam.q: A wire of length 0.050 m carries a current of 3.0 A at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.20 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
exam.tip: Substitution then answer with unit.

exam.q: The current in a wire in a magnetic field is doubled. All other factors stay the same. State what happens to the force on the wire.
model: The force doubles.
exam.tip: Use 'doubles', not just 'increases'.

exam.q: Give two ways of increasing the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field without changing its direction.
model: Increase the current.
Use a stronger magnet / increase the magnetic flux density.
Increase the length of wire in the field (any two).
exam.tip: Avoid 'bigger magnet'; say stronger.

exam.q: A force of 0.048 N acts on a wire carrying 4.0 A at right angles to a field of 0.30 T. Calculate the length of wire in the field. Give your answer in cm.
model: l = F / (B x I)
exam.tip: Answer in the unit asked for - convert at the end.

exam.q: A wire of length 6.0 cm lies at right angles to a field of 150 mT. The force on it is 0.018 N. Calculate the current.
model: Convert: l = 0.060 m, B = 0.150 T
exam.tip: Two conversions hidden in one question.

exam.q: Explain why a wire placed parallel to a magnetic field experiences no force even when it carries a current.
model: The force (F = BIl) only acts when the wire has a component at right angles to the field / is at an angle to the field lines.
When parallel, the current and the field are in the same direction, so the force is zero.
exam.tip: Mention the right-angle condition.

exam.q: A student plots a graph of force F against current I for a wire of length 0.25 m in a uniform field. The gradient is 0.050 N/A. Calculate the magnetic flux density.
model: Gradient = F / I = B x l
B = gradient / l = 0.050 / 0.25
exam.tip: Identify what the gradient represents before calculating.

exam.q: A magnet on a top-pan balance has a fixed wire passing between its poles at right angles to the field. When the current is 2.5 A the balance reading increases by 1.5 g. The length of wire in the field is 4.0 cm. Calculate the magnetic flux density. (g = 10 N/kg)
exam.tip: Two conversions (g to kg, cm to m) and two equations: keep the steps clearly separated.

exam.q: Describe an experiment to investigate how the force on a current-carrying wire in a magnetic field depends on the current in the wire.
model: Place a magnet on a top-pan balance and zero (tare) the balance.
Clamp a straight wire between the poles, at right angles to the field, so it cannot touch the magnet or move.
Connect the wire in series with a d.c. supply, ammeter and variable resistor (rheostat).
Switch on, set a current and record the current and the change in balance reading; force = mass change (kg) x 10 N/kg.
Repeat for a range of at least five currents, keeping the magnet and length of wire in the field the same (control variables); switch off between readings to avoid heating.
Repeat and average, then plot F against I; a straight line through the origin shows F is directly proportional to I.
exam.tip: Six-mark method answers need equipment, what you measure, how you get the force, control variables, safety/repeats and how you analyse the results.

worked.q: A straight wire carries a current of 4.0 A. 8.0 cm of it lies at right angles to a magnetic field of flux density 0.25 T. Calculate the force on the wire.
steps: Write the equation: F = B x I x l.
Convert the length: 8.0 cm = 0.080 m.
Substitute: F = 0.25 T x 4.0 A x 0.080 m.
Calculate: F = 0.080 N.

worked.q: A force of 0.036 N acts on a 12 cm length of wire at right angles to a field of 150 mT. Calculate the current in the wire.
steps: Rearrange: I = F / (B x l).
Convert: l = 12 cm = 0.12 m; B = 150 mT = 0.15 T.
Bottom line: 0.15 x 0.12 = 0.018.

worked.q: In a top-pan balance experiment the reading changes by 3.0 g when a current of 2.0 A flows in a fixed wire with 5.0 cm of its length in the field. Find the magnetic flux density and predict the change in reading if the current is increased to 5.0 A. (g = 10 N/kg)
steps: Mass change in kg: 3.0 g = 0.0030 kg.
Force: F = m x g = 0.0030 x 10 = 0.030 N (equal to the force on the wire by Newton's third law).
Length: 5.0 cm = 0.050 m.
F is directly proportional to I, so at 5.0 A: F = 0.030 x (5.0 / 2.0) = 0.075 N.
Change in reading = 0.075 / 10 = 0.0075 kg = 7.5 g.
worked.ans: B = 0.30 T; the reading would change by 7.5 g.

phy_edx.11.5.summary: An electric motor uses the **motor effect** to produce **rotation**. A coil of wire carrying a current sits in a magnetic field; because the current flows in **opposite directions** along the two sides of the coil, the forces on those sides are in **opposite directions**, producing a **turning effect (moment)** about the axle. A **split-ring commutator** reverses the current in the coil every **half turn**, so the forces keep turning the coil the same way and it rotates continuously. The speed and turning force can be increased with a bigger current, a stronger magnetic field or more turns on the coil, and the direction of rotation is reversed by reversing the current or the field.

core.h: From a force on a wire to rotation
core.p: A straight wire in a magnetic field is pushed in one direction. To get continuous **rotation** instead, a motor bends the wire into a **rectangular coil** mounted on an **axle** between the poles of a magnet. The two long sides of the coil both cut across the field but carry current in **opposite directions**.
bullets: Current goes **along one side** of the coil and **back along the other side**, so the currents in the two sides are opposite.
By Fleming's left-hand rule, opposite currents in the same field give **opposite forces**: one side is pushed **up**, the other **down**.
Two equal, opposite forces acting on opposite sides of an axle form a **turning effect (moment)**, so the coil **rotates** about the axle.
The short sides of the coil that run **parallel** to the field experience **no force**.
This is how a motor transfers energy from the **electrical** store/supply to the **kinetic** store of the rotating coil.

callouts.p: The forces on the two sides of the coil are in **opposite directions** because the **current flows in opposite directions** in the two sides. This causes the coil to **rotate**.

core.h: Parts of a simple d.c. motor
core.p: You need to name each part and say what it does. Edexcel mark schemes reward the specific job of each part.
bullets: **Coil** of insulated wire (many turns) on an **axle**: the part that rotates.
**Permanent magnets** (or electromagnets) with N and S poles facing each other: provide a magnetic field across the coil.
**Split-ring commutator**: a ring split into two halves, each connected to one end of the coil; it rotates with the coil and **reverses the current in the coil every half turn**.
**Brushes** (usually carbon): stationary contacts that press on the commutator and connect the rotating coil to the external circuit.
**d.c. supply** (battery or power pack): provides the current.

core.h: Using Fleming's left-hand rule on the coil
core.p: Looking at the coil end-on (along the axle), one side has current going into the page and the other has current coming out. Apply the rule to each side separately.
bullets: Field from N (left) to S (right): First finger points right.
Side with current **into** the page (cross): thumb points **down**, so the force is downwards.
Side with current **out of** the page (dot): thumb points **up**, so the force is upwards.
Left side down + right side up = the coil turns **anticlockwise** in this view.
If you reverse the current (or the field) both forces reverse and the coil turns clockwise.

callouts.p: When asked to draw the forces on a coil, draw one arrow on each long side, in opposite directions, at right angles to the field lines. Do not draw arrows on the sides parallel to the field.

core.p: If the coil were connected directly to the supply (with the wires twisting), it would not keep spinning. Understanding why is the key to explaining the commutator.
bullets: The forces on each side are always **up/down** (vertical) because the field is horizontal.
When the coil reaches the **vertical position**, the forces act **along a line through the axle**, so there is **no turning effect**.
Momentum carries the coil slightly past vertical. Now the side that was pushed up is on top, still being pushed up, so the force turns it **back**.
The coil would just **rock back and forth** and come to rest in the vertical position.
Solution: **reverse the current** in the coil just as it passes vertical, so the forces swap direction and keep it turning the same way.

core.p: The **split-ring commutator** is a metal ring cut into two halves, insulated from each other, fixed to the axle so it spins with the coil. Each half is joined to one end of the coil. Two fixed brushes press on opposite sides of it.
bullets: Every **half turn**, the halves of the ring swap from touching one brush to touching the other.
This **reverses the direction of the current in the coil** every half turn.
The swap happens when the coil is about **vertical** (where the turning effect is zero anyway), which is where the gaps in the ring pass the brushes.
Result: the side of the coil that is on the left (say) **always** has current in the same direction, so it is **always pushed the same way**.
So the coil keeps turning in the **same direction**: continuous rotation.
The current in the external circuit stays d.c.; only the current **in the coil** reverses.

callouts.p: The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so that the forces on the coil keep it rotating in the same direction.

callouts.t: It does not reverse the supply
callouts.p: Do not say the commutator 'changes d.c. to a.c.' or 'reverses the battery'. It reverses the current in the coil relative to the coil.

core.p: The coil is spinning but the supply wires are fixed, so something has to make a **sliding electrical contact**.
bullets: Brushes are usually made of **carbon (graphite)**: it conducts electricity and is soft and slippery, so it rubs against the commutator with little friction.
Springs press the brushes against the commutator to keep a good contact.
They stop the supply wires from **twisting** as the coil turns.
Brushes wear away over time and must be replaced; sparking at the brushes wastes energy.

core.h: One complete revolution, step by step
core.p: Being able to describe what happens through a full turn is a typical 4 to 6 mark task.
bullets: **Coil horizontal** (plane parallel to the field): forces on the sides are at maximum distance from the axle, so the **turning effect is maximum**.
**Coil turning towards vertical**: forces stay the same size but act closer to the line of the axle, so the turning effect **decreases**.
**Coil vertical**: forces act through the axle, so the **turning effect is zero**; the gaps in the commutator pass the brushes and the **current in the coil reverses**.
The coil's **momentum** carries it past the vertical position.
**After vertical**: the reversed current means the forces again turn the coil the same way; the turning effect builds back to maximum at horizontal.
This repeats every half turn, so the coil keeps rotating.

core.h: Why the turning effect depends on position
core.p: A turning effect (moment) depends on both the force and its **perpendicular distance from the pivot**: moment = force x perpendicular distance from the pivot.
bullets: The force on each side stays roughly the same size (F = BIl) because the side is always at right angles to the field.
What changes is the **perpendicular distance** between the line of the force and the axle.
Horizontal coil: perpendicular distance = half the coil width (maximum), so maximum moment.
Vertical coil: the force passes through the axle, perpendicular distance = 0, so zero moment.
This makes a simple motor's turning effect uneven; real motors use several coils at different angles for a smoother, steadier turning effect.

core.h: Making the motor turn faster or with more force
core.p: Anything that increases the force on each side of the coil increases the turning effect, so the motor speeds up (or can lift a bigger load).
bullets: **Increase the current** in the coil (increase the p.d. of the supply).
**Use a stronger magnetic field** (stronger magnets, or electromagnets).
**Increase the number of turns** on the coil: each turn adds its own force, so the total force on each side is multiplied.
Make the coil **longer** (more length in the field) or **wider** (forces act further from the axle, increasing the moment).
Wind the coil on a **soft iron core** (armature), which concentrates the magnetic field through the coil.

callouts.p: Every speed factor comes straight from F = B x I x l: bigger B, bigger I or more effective length l (more turns) gives a bigger force on each side.

core.p: The direction of the forces depends on the directions of the current and the field, so the direction of rotation does too.
bullets: **Reverse the current**: swap the connections to the supply (turn the battery round).
**Reverse the magnetic field**: swap the positions of the N and S poles.
Doing **both** at once leaves the motor turning the **same** way.
Turning the supply voltage up or down changes speed, not direction.

callouts.p: A common trap: 'reverse the battery and swap the magnets' gives no change in direction.

core.p: A motor is an energy-transferring device. Mark schemes accept the energy-store language from Topic 1.
bullets: Useful transfer: energy is transferred **electrically** from the supply to the **kinetic energy store** of the coil (and anything it drives, e.g. lifting a load into a gravitational store).
Wasted energy: **thermal** energy from the resistance of the coil (heating effect of current), friction at the axle bearings and brushes, and **sound**.
Efficiency = useful energy output / total energy input (can be given as a percentage).
Reduce waste with lubricated bearings, low-resistance (thick copper) wire and good brush contact.

core.p: Electric motors appear in almost every device that turns or moves using electricity.
bullets: Fans, washing machines, food mixers, electric drills and power tools.
Electric cars, trains, lifts and cranes.
Computer hard drives, DVD players and toy cars.
In each case: current in a coil + magnetic field = forces on the coil = rotation.

callouts.p: Current in coil -> coil sides in magnetic field -> forces (motor effect) -> opposite directions on each side (opposite currents) -> turning effect -> commutator reverses current every half turn -> continuous rotation in same direction.

analogy.p: The two sides of the coil are like your two feet on the pedals: one pushes down while the other comes up, and together they turn the crank (the axle). When a pedal is at the very top or bottom, pushing straight down does nothing (like the coil at vertical, where the forces go through the axle), and momentum carries you through this dead spot. The commutator is like your legs automatically swapping which foot pushes down every half turn, so the crank always goes the same way. Where it breaks down: your feet push in whatever direction you choose, but the magnetic forces are always at right angles to the field and only reverse because the current in the coil is reversed by the commutator.

terms.d: A device that uses the motor effect on a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field to produce rotation.
A current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field experiences a force.
Insulated wire wound in loops (turns), mounted on an axle so that it can rotate in the magnetic field.
The rod through the centre of the coil about which the coil rotates (the pivot).
A ring split into two insulated halves, attached to the coil ends, which reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn.
Fixed carbon contacts that press against the rotating commutator to connect the coil to the supply.
The turning effect of a force about a pivot: force x perpendicular distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force.
Rotation through 180 degrees; the commutator reverses the coil current once every half turn.
The tendency of the moving coil to keep turning, which carries it past the vertical position where the turning effect is zero.
The rotating part of a motor: the coil wound on a soft iron core.
A core that is easily magnetised and concentrates the magnetic field through the coil, increasing the force.
How many loops of wire make up the coil; more turns give a bigger total force on each side.
Thumb = force/motion, first finger = field, second finger = current; used to find the force direction on each side of the coil.
Current that flows in one direction only, as supplied by a battery to a simple motor.
Useful energy output divided by total energy input; motors waste energy as heat, sound and through friction.

mistakes.r: The commutator reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn.

mistakes.w: The forces on both sides of the coil are in the same direction.
mistakes.r: The forces are in opposite directions because the current is in opposite directions in the two sides.

mistakes.w: The commutator reverses the current every full turn.
mistakes.r: Every half turn.

mistakes.w: The coil is attracted to the magnets and that makes it spin.
mistakes.r: Current in the coil in the magnetic field produces forces (motor effect) that create a turning effect.

mistakes.w: To make it spin faster use a bigger magnet.
mistakes.r: Use a stronger magnet / stronger magnetic field (or increase the current, or more turns).

mistakes.w: Reversing the battery and the magnets reverses the motor.
mistakes.r: Reversing both leaves the direction unchanged; reverse only one.

mistakes.w: The turning effect is greatest when the coil is vertical.
mistakes.r: Greatest when the coil is horizontal (parallel to the field); zero when vertical.

exam.q: Name the part of a d.c. motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn.
model: Split-ring commutator.
exam.tip: Say 'split-ring', not just 'ring'.

exam.q: State what the brushes in a d.c. motor are usually made of.
model: Carbon / graphite.
exam.tip: Remember why: it conducts and is slippery.

exam.q: State two ways to make a d.c. motor turn faster.
model: Increase the current / increase the p.d.
Use a stronger magnet / stronger magnetic field.
Increase the number of turns on the coil (any two).
exam.tip: Two separate factors, each a mark.

exam.q: State two ways to reverse the direction of rotation of a d.c. motor.
model: Reverse the direction of the current (swap the battery connections).
Reverse the magnetic field (swap the magnet poles).
exam.tip: Never both at once.

exam.q: Explain why the two sides of the coil in a motor experience forces in opposite directions.
model: The current flows in opposite directions in the two sides of the coil.
The field is the same direction, so (by Fleming's left-hand rule) the forces are opposite.
exam.tip: Key idea: opposite currents in the same field.

exam.q: Explain why there is no turning effect on the coil when it is vertical.
model: The forces on the sides act along a line through the axle / pivot.
So the perpendicular distance is zero and the moment is zero.
exam.tip: Use 'moment' or 'turning effect' and 'axle'.

exam.q: Explain why the coil continues to rotate through the vertical position.
model: The coil has momentum, which carries it past the vertical.
The commutator then reverses the current so the forces turn it the same way.
exam.tip: Two ideas: momentum and the commutator.

exam.q: Explain the purpose of the split-ring commutator in a d.c. motor.
model: It reverses the direction of the current in the coil.
Every half turn (as the coil passes vertical).
So the forces on each side keep turning the coil in the same direction / continuous rotation.
exam.tip: Say what, when, and why it matters.

exam.q: Describe what would happen to a simple motor if the split-ring commutator were replaced by two complete slip rings (so the current in the coil never reversed).
model: The coil would turn until it reached the vertical position.
Past vertical the forces would act to turn it back.

exam.q: Explain how a simple d.c. motor works. Your answer should refer to the forces on the coil and the role of the commutator.
model: A current flows through the coil which is in the magnetic field of the magnets.
Each side of the coil experiences a force (motor effect), whose direction is given by Fleming's left-hand rule.
The current is in opposite directions in the two sides, so the forces are in opposite directions (one up, one down).
This produces a turning effect / moment about the axle, so the coil rotates.
When the coil is vertical the turning effect is zero; momentum carries it past.
The split-ring commutator reverses the current in the coil every half turn so the coil keeps rotating in the same direction; brushes keep contact with the rotating commutator.
exam.tip: Work round the motor in a logical order: current, force, opposite forces, rotation, commutator. Use the exact names of the parts.

worked.q: Model answer: A student's model motor turns slowly. Suggest and explain three changes that would make it turn faster.
steps: Increase the current (raise the supply p.d.): the force on each side, F = BIl, increases with I.
Use stronger magnets: a bigger flux density B increases the force on each side.
Add more turns to the coil: each turn contributes a force, so the total force on each side increases.
A bigger force on each side gives a bigger turning effect, so the coil speeds up.
worked.ans: Increase the current, use a stronger magnetic field and increase the number of turns; each increases the force on the coil sides and so the turning effect.

worked.q: A coil has 50 turns. Each long side has 4.0 cm in a field of 0.20 T and the current is 0.50 A. The sides are 1.5 cm from the axle. Calculate the force on one side and the total moment when the coil is horizontal.
steps: Force on one wire: F = B x I x l = 0.20 x 0.50 x 0.040 = 0.0040 N.
50 turns act together: force on one side = 50 x 0.0040 = 0.20 N.
Coil horizontal: perpendicular distance from axle = 1.5 cm = 0.015 m.
Moment from one side = 0.20 x 0.015 = 0.0030 N m.
Both sides turn the coil the same way: total moment = 2 x 0.0030 = 0.0060 N m.
worked.ans: Force on each side = 0.20 N; total moment = 0.0060 N m (maximum, as the coil is horizontal).

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why the turning effect on the coil of a simple motor changes as it rotates from horizontal to vertical.
steps: The force on each side stays the same size because each side stays at right angles to the field.
The forces are always vertical (perpendicular to the horizontal field).
As the coil turns towards vertical, the line of each force moves closer to the axle.
So the perpendicular distance, and hence the moment, decreases, reaching zero when the coil is vertical.
worked.ans: The turning effect falls from a maximum (horizontal) to zero (vertical) because the perpendicular distance between the forces and the axle decreases, even though the forces stay the same size.
